newsitem.title: USA: Chateau sees no merit in suit.
newsitem.headline: Chateau sees no merit in suit.

text.p: Mobile home park operator Chateau Properties Inc said Thursday a lawsuit filed against it by unsolicited suitor Manufactured Home Communities Inc has no merit.
"There is no merit to their lawsuit and we're in court today to defend our position," said Jeff Kellogg, chief executive and president of Chateau.

Manufactured, a real estate investment trust led by investor Sam Zell, on Wednesday filed suit against Chateau and various board members, and ROC Communities Inc over a pending merger between Chateau and ROC.
Chateau rejected unsolicited merger offers from MHC and Sun Communities Inc and urged shareholders not to accept MHC's all-cash tender offer of $26 a share.
After receiving the unsolicited offers, Chateau went back to ROC and revised a merger the two agreed on in July.

In a U.S. District Court in Maryland, MHC filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order to prevent Chateau from repurchasing 1.45 million shares as approved by its board and to keep ROC from purchasing 350,000 shares.

The stock purchases are necessary to implement a tax code included in the merger plans, allowing operating unit holders to convert units into shares on a tax-free basis. Without it, the OP unit holders would face stiff capital gains taxes.
In a telephone interview, Kellogg said he expects a decision today on the request, the only point argued today.
"We weren't doing it anyway," Kellogg said, referring to the approved repurchase plan. "But there is nothing to prevent us from doing a self tender or negotiated transaction."
MHC charged Chateau misrepresented material facts to block MHC's tender offer.

The suit alleges the proposed merger disenfranchises Chateau shareholders by reducing the voting requirement and manipulating the vote. In addition, MHC charged the merger would transfer a deferred taxable gain of more than $100 million from insiders to shareholders.
Kellogg denied the charges and said the number is more like $10 million for Chateau shareholders and $20 million for ROC shareholders.
"The only way that will figure in to all the shareholders would be if all the properties were sold," he said, adding Chateau has not sold property in at least than 10 years.
"We're in the business of buying and managing properties," Kellogg said, adding that if a property were to be sold, "the tax consequence is negligible."

He said the company's two independent advisors, Goldman Sachs and Merrill Lynch, both found the MHC offer inadequate. In the past he has said the company is not for sale and, if it were, it would expect more than $26 a share.

"The advisors also advised the board that the ROC revised merger was very fair to the shareholders," Kellogg said. "The board absolutely fulfilled its fiduciary duty to its shareholders and OP unit holders."
